title: Are they equal?
hook: are those who know and those who don't know equal (39:9)
carry: knowing isn't equal to not knowing

segments.voice: Yesterday, Iblis asks for time, and your line was the sincere are protected. Did you do one thing today that nobody will ever hear about? Today, a new surah, Az-Zumar. Day five hundred fifty-eight.

Some questions don't need an answer. Is water wet? Would you rather be warm or freezing? A teacher asks one in class and nobody raises a hand, because the answer is sitting right there in the question. The Qur'an uses this kind of question often, and Surah Az-Zumar, the thirty-ninth, has one of the most quoted. It's carved over the doors of libraries and schools across the Muslim world. But the verse it comes from begins somewhere you might not expect: not in a classroom, but in the middle of the night.
screen: `IT STARTS IN THE MIDDLE OF THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Verse nine opens with a picture. Someone is up in the hours of the night, bowing down and standing in prayer, wary of the hereafter, hoping for the mercy of their Lord. Is that person like the one who isn't? Then the famous line. Pickthall: "Are those who know equal with those who know not? But only men of understanding will pay heed." The answer is built in: no. But look at what knowing means here. It's not trivia. It sits right after the night prayer, the fear, the hope. Many commentators say the knowing in this verse is knowing your Lord, and acting on it: the person who knows why they're awake at three in the morning. So the verse joins two things people often split: learning and devotion. And the tradition took that seriously. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says that whoever walks a path seeking knowledge, Allah makes easy for them a path to paradise. Another, in Ibn Majah, says seeking knowledge is an obligation on every Muslim, and scholars point out that every means every, men and women alike. That's part of why the first universities in many Muslim cities grew out of mosques, and why this verse ends up over library doors. Then the last phrase: only people of understanding, ulu'l-albab, will take it to heart. Lubb means a kernel, the inner core of a nut. People of understanding are people who get to the core of things. Knowing and not knowing aren't the same. But the verse adds: it takes some knowing even to notice that.
screen: `A PATH TO KNOWLEDGE, A PATH TO PARADISE.`

segments.voice: The outline's practice is to read for ten minutes. Begin now, small. If you have a book nearby, a Qur'an, a history, anything worth learning from, open it and read one page slowly, as if you'll be asked about it. If not, think of one subject you've always meant to understand better, and choose the first thing you'll read about it. Then sit with what you read, or what you chose, and let it settle to its kernel. The bell holds the time.
Are they equal? Surah Az-Zumar's question: are those who know equal to those who don't, asked right after a picture of someone praying at night. Today's word.
Your line: knowing isn't equal to not knowing. Today, find ten minutes, and read something that makes you know a little more than this morning. Day five hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Muslims treat seeking knowledge as a religious duty; many attend study circles (halaqas) at mosques, and 39:9 is often inscribed on schools and libraries.

original.note: Arabic: are they equal? a question the Qur'an asks often, with the answer built in.

trapdoor: what you thought: smart people beat less-smart people.
what it means: knowing your Lord and acting on it, like the person praying at night, isn't the same as not knowing.
what a scholar hears: 39:9 joins qunut at night with 'ilm; ulu'l-albab from lubb, the kernel; the hadith on the path to knowledge is Muslim 2699 and 'an obligation on every Muslim' is Ibn Majah 224.
